<!-- BEAT 2 — Discipline 1: Earn complexity -->

## *Each unit of complexity is earned — by a documented failure of the simpler model.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-10_02.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Disciplina **uno**. Prima riga del notebook, *prima* del training: *baseline = logistic regression su $5$–$10$ feature scelte clinicamente, target = AUPRC $\ge 0.30$, escalate solo se il baseline fallisce sul validation*. Lo stop-criterion va scritto **prima** — scritto *dopo* è razionalizzazione, non disciplina. La complessità si **guadagna**: ogni unità di parametri in più va pagata in robustezza, interpretabilità, rischio di overfitting. Sali la scala (rung $1$ = logistic, rung $2$ = tree, rung $3$ = RF, rung $4$ = GB, rung $5$ = NN) **solo quando il rung sotto ha fallito documentato**. Il *signed-before* + *fail-to-climb* + *bottom-glows-brightest* è la *triade visiva* della disciplina.
:::

## Earn complexity — write the rule *before* training {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**The first three lines of the planning document — written *before* any model is trained.**

1. **Baseline** — *the simplest model on the smallest sensible feature set*. E.g. logistic regression on $5$–$10$ clinically-chosen features (*age, ICU LOS, Charlson, prior $90$-day admissions, eGFR at discharge, number of medications*).
2. **Baseline metric $+$ target** — *a number the baseline could plausibly reach.* E.g. AUPRC $\ge 0.30$ on the held-out **validation** split (or recall $\ge 0.60$ at precision $\ge 0.30$).
3. **Escalation rule** — *one named failure, one named direction, one named "ship the baseline" branch.* E.g. *"if the baseline reaches the target on validation, **ship the baseline**; otherwise escalate to gradient boosting on a wider clinical feature set."*

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Why the rule must be written *ex ante*.**

> Written *before* the run, the rule **constrains** the run. Written *after*, it is a *rationalisation* of decisions already made — and the ethics committee will read it as such.

A binding stop-criterion has **two** real branches: *escalate* **and** *ship the baseline*. If the target is rigged so high that only *escalate* can ever fire, the rule has collapsed into a *plan disguised as a rule*.

*More parameters and richer features are paid for in robustness, interpretability, and risk of overfitting — so each added unit of complexity must be earned by a failure of the simpler model.*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
La tabella operativa di Obj. $1$. Il punto pedagogico che porta il peso: la *temporalità* della stop-criterion. Scriverla *prima* è disciplina; scriverla *dopo* è razionalizzazione — è esattamente il distrattore A dell'item $01$ (Marco scrive la stop-criterion nei *Methods* dopo aver visto entrambi i risultati). Il distrattore D dell'item $01$ è la versione più sottile: target *sintatticamente corretto* ($0.80$) ma *irraggiungibile* su $p = 5\%$ — l'*if-then* ha solo un ramo reale (escalate). La stop-criterion deve avere *due rami reali*, altrimenti è un *piano travestito da regola*. Reveal-only: in classe leggo solo i tre punti della colonna sinistra e la box-quote sulla destra; il resto lo sa il deck.
:::

<!-- BEAT 3 — Discipline 2: Protect the test -->

## *$95\%$ on $p = 5\%$ is the trap; the test is opened exactly once.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-10_03.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Disciplina **due**, in due regole che vivono insieme. **R$1$** — *accuracy trap*: l'*accuracy meter pegged at the top* è cablato a *una sola classe* della distribuzione $95\%$ / $5\%$ — la metrica è *rotta* prima che la voce docente lo dica. **R$2$** — *leakage rule*: il *locked drawer* + le *ghostly hands* bloccate da una *warm-orange chain* + il *$1\times$-only marker* è la visualizzazione operativa del *protect the test*. Il *connector "R1 + R2"* in basso lega le due metà: **una disciplina, due regole**.
:::

## Protect the test — two rules, one discipline {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**R$1$ — accuracy trap.**

On a prevalence $p$, the *always-predict-majority* classifier reaches accuracy $1 - p$ with $0$ recall on the rare class. On $p = 5\%$ that is $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ — *statistically brilliant, clinically useless*.

- discard *accuracy* on imbalanced data;
- choose **AUPRC**, **F$1$**, or **recall at a target precision**;
- set the threshold on the **clinical cost ratio** of FP vs FN, not on a curve in isolation.

*The relevant baseline on imbalanced data is **always-predict-NO**, not a coin-flip.*

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**R$2$ — leakage rule.**

> *Any decision (model, hyperparameter, feature set, threshold) taken **after** having seen a performance number on a dataset converts that dataset into a training set — even if the file is labelled "test".*

The test is **looked at exactly once, at the end, and never again**.

- the trigger is the **decision**, not the *observation*;
- contamination is **retrospective** — no procedure applied afterwards repairs the original test;
- the fix for a contaminated test is a **new** held-out split, not a fresh validation.

*A fresh **validation** split is where thresholding and tuning live; the test stays in the drawer.*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Le due regole di Obj. $2$. **R$1$** è l'item $02$ (Sara presenta $94.8\%$ di accuracy, *exactly inside the always-predict-NO band*) — distrattori canonici: $80\%$ = prevalenza letta male; $50\%$ = confusione baseline-random con baseline-majority; $100\%$ = confusione accuracy con true-negative rate. **R$2$** è l'item $03$ (Davide guarda il test, bumpa L$2$, riguarda il test) — il punto sottile è che la regola si attiva sul *decidere*, non sul *guardare*; e la contaminazione è *retrospettiva*: un *fresh validation split* (item $03$ distrattore D) fixa il futuro ma **non** ripara il test già contaminato — serve un *new test*, non solo una *fresh validation*. Reveal-only sui dettagli matematici della baseline-on-prevalence; leggo a voce solo le due frasi-box.
:::

<!-- BEAT 4 — Discipline 3: Match interpretability -->

## *Linear → coefficients; tree → path; ensemble → SHAP — the tradeoff is clinical.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-10_04.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Disciplina **tre**. La tecnica di interpretabilità segue la **famiglia del modello** (mappatura $1{:}1$, colonna sinistra → colonna destra). La connessione *RF/GB ↔ variable importance + SHAP* è in warm orange acceso: è la coppia che la narrativa sceglie (Elena ship un gradient boosting con SHAP, non una logistic cieca). **Crucially**: la *balance-scale* a destra con il *clinical-lead silhouette* in posa di pivot — il tradeoff *interpretability vs performance* **non è una scelta tecnica**, è una **scelta clinica**, e la prende il clinical lead, non il data scientist. Slide *reveal-only* in classe (lascio respirare l'immagine $\sim 5$ secondi e cito a voce solo la signature line *"the tradeoff is clinical"*); la tabella espansiva la lasci al deck per consultazione asincrona.
:::

## Match interpretability — the $1{:}1$ mapping {.smaller}

| Model family | Built-in / Post-hoc | Interpretability technique | What you read off |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Linear / logistic regression** | built-in | **coefficients** | log-odds change per unit feature, with sign and magnitude |
| **Decision tree** (single) | built-in | **decision path** | a sequence of human-readable *if-then* rules |
| **Random forest / gradient boosting** | post-hoc | **variable importance** $+$ SHAP for case-level | global ranking; per-patient attribution |
| **Neural network / deep model** | post-hoc | **SHAP** or surrogate models | per-sample additive attribution |

**The clinical-defensibility rule, one sentence:**

> *If the deployment requires clinical defensibility, prefer a model whose interpretability is **built-in** — **unless** the performance gap to the opaque model is large enough that the patient is better off with the box-with-attribution than with a simpler model that misclassifies more often. The tradeoff is a clinical decision, not a technical one.*

*The committee's question is not "is the model interpretable?" — it is "why **this** model on **this** patient?". The answer is owed to the **patient**, before the committee even asks.*

::: {.notes}
La regola operativa di Obj. $3$. **Mossa critica**: la *scelta* del livello di interpretabilità è **clinica**, non tecnica — se il SHAP-su-forest cattura abbastanza readmission da giustificare la perdita di interpretabilità built-in, il paziente è meglio servito dal *box con attribution* che dal *semplice cieco*. Il giudizio è del *clinical lead*, non del data scientist. Item $04$ (applicativa): la risposta *invertita* — *"revert to logistic + coefficients because the extra recall is below the cost-ratio threshold"* — è **accettata a Excellent** se il framing clinico è ben posto. La rubrica misura *applicare il tradeoff come scelta clinica*, non *scegliere random forest*.
:::

## Summative — *Monday's audit, Friday's defence* {.inverse .smaller background-color="#1F4257"}

**Scenario.** *Build a model for $30$-day readmission after ICU discharge. $5\,000$ patients · $50$ candidate features · prevalence $p \approx 5\%$ · defence to the clinical lead $+$ ethics committee in three weeks. They will ask: "why this model? why this metric? why should I trust it on my next patient?"*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Fill the three-section planning sheet — three sub-tasks per section:**

| § | Section | Sub-tasks |
|---|---|---|
| **$1$** | first iteration | baseline · metric $+$ target · stop-criterion |
| **$2$** | metric $+$ leakage | metric $+$ why-not-accuracy · threshold rule · leakage trap |
| **$3$** | model $+$ interpretability | final model if baseline fails · interpretability that *matches* · $1$-sentence clinical defence |

Plus **one sentence**: *"Why this model?"*

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Two live polls (Slido — individual):**

- **Poll $1$** — *On this dataset, what is the accuracy of always-predict-NO-readmission?* — $50\%$ / $80\%$ / $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ / $100\%$;
- **Poll $2$** — *You see test accuracy $92\%$, bump L$2$, re-check the test: $93\%$. Is the second number faithful?* — yes / $\boldsymbol{\text{no, model changed after a test number}}$ / yes if both reported / only after a fresh validation.

*Time: $\sim 9$′ (min $6$–$15$ — end of course). Banco unico condiviso, presenza $+$ remoto.*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Sommativo — gira negli ultimi $\sim 9$′ (min $6$–$15$). $\sim 1$′ leggi scenario + apri polls + $\sim 2$′$30$″ fill Section $1$ (baseline + metric/target + stop-criterion) [Poll $1$ chiude min $10$ o $\geq 80\%$, hard cap $90$″] + $\sim 2$′$30$″ Section $2$ (metric + threshold + leakage trap) [Poll $2$ chiude min $12$ o $\geq 80\%$] + $\sim 1$′$30$″ Section $3$ (final model + interpretability + clinical defence) + $\sim 1$′$30$″ instructor-led reveal. **Distrattori Poll $1$** nominati nel reveal: $50\%$ = "ha confuso baseline-random con baseline-majority"; $80\%$ = "ha letto la prevalenza come $20\%$ invece di $5\%$"; $100\%$ = "ha confuso *accuracy* con *true-negative rate*". La risposta corretta $95\%$ si legge da $1 - 0.05$. **Distrattori Poll $2$**: *yes* = "non ha applicato R$2$"; *yes if both reported* = "ha confuso trasparenza con correttezza"; *only after a fresh validation* = "ha la soluzione operativa ma non la regola — la *correzione* è usare un *new test*, non solo una *fresh validation*". **Nota di tempistica**: per liberare $9$′ al sommativo la fase espositiva va portata a $\sim 6$′ — leggo a voce solo *KISS / iterate*, *accuracy trap*, *leakage rule*; *interpretability* e *Modern Alchemist* restano *reveal-only* (la classe le legge sul deck).
:::

## Summative — canonical solution {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

**Section $1$.** Baseline $=$ *logistic regression on $6$ clinically-chosen features* (age, ICU LOS, Charlson, prior $90$-day admissions, eGFR, $\#$ medications). Target $=$ *AUPRC $\ge 0.30$ on validation*. Stop-criterion (*written ex ante*) $=$ *if baseline reaches target, ship the baseline; otherwise escalate to gradient boosting on a wider clinical feature set*.

**Section $2$.** Metric $=$ *AUPRC $+$ recall-at-precision* (not accuracy — *always-predict-NO scores $95\%$, recall $0$*). Threshold $=$ *set on the clinical cost ratio the clinical lead signs off on* (missed readmission $\ne$ false alarm). Leakage trap $=$ *thresholding on the test* / *peeking after L$2$ change* — fix: **fresh validation split** for tuning; test **sealed in a drawer** until the day of the defence.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Section $3$.** Final model $=$ *gradient boosting on $\sim 12$ clinically-chosen features* (because the baseline missed by $0.03$ AUPRC). Interpretability $=$ **variable importance** $+$ per-patient SHAP attribution against the patient's chart. *Why this model?* — *"because a missed readmission costs $\sim 3\times$ a false alarm, and the simpler model misses too many — the clinical lead accepted the loss of built-in interpretability for the recall margin."*

**Live signal of mastery.** The class reads off the board, without prompting: *start simple, measure honestly, defend clinically — and on this scenario the answer is **logistic** if the baseline reaches $0.30$, **gradient boosting + variable importance** otherwise. The three disciplines compose; they do not stack as four patches.*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Reveal finale del sommativo. Voce docente sulla regola di ordine superiore: *"sai che le best practice non sono un menu — sono un **ordine di operazioni**. Senza la prima (stop-criterion ex ante), qualunque modello complicato è una scommessa non motivata. Senza la seconda (metrica per il problema che hai + test sigillato), qualunque numero su qualunque slide è dubbio. Senza la terza (interpretability matched + tradeoff clinico), qualunque sistema 'che funziona' è indifendibile al primo paziente che chiede 'perché lei mi ha dimesso/non dimesso'."* La frase *"the three disciplines compose; they do not stack as four patches"* è il take-home dell'item $05$ (la critica al piano di Anna) — pre-shadowing dell'argomentativa.
:::

<!-- Item 01 — MCQ — Stop-criterion ex ante -->

## Item 01 — Question {.smaller}

Marco is about to start an audit on **$30$-day ICU readmission** ($5\,000$ patients · $50$ features · $p \approx 5\%$ · defence in three weeks). He shows you four versions of the *Methods* — four ways of writing the **stop-criterion** that *earn complexity* asks for. **Which one applies the discipline correctly?**

- **A)** Marco trains *logistic regression on $6$ features* (validation AUPRC $0.27$), then *gradient boosting on the same features* (validation AUPRC $0.31$). With both results in front of him he writes: *"We adopted gradient boosting because logistic regression failed to reach the AUPRC target we had set for the baseline."*
- **B)** *Before* training: *"We will train **gradient boosting on $30$ features** as our primary model — gradient boosting consistently outperforms logistic regression on tabular clinical data. We will report AUPRC and recall on the test set. If unsatisfactory, we will revisit the modelling choice."*
- **C)** *Before* training: *"Baseline: **logistic regression on $6$ clinically-chosen features**. Target: **AUPRC $\ge 0.30$** on validation. Escalation: if the baseline does not reach AUPRC $0.30$ on validation, escalate to gradient boosting on a wider feature set; **if the baseline reaches the target, ship the baseline**."*
- **D)** *Before* training: *"Baseline: logistic regression on $6$ features. Target: **AUPRC $\ge 0.80$** on validation. Escalation: if the baseline does not reach $0.80$, escalate to gradient boosting."*

::: {.notes}
Item $01$ — Comprehension / MCQ / medium. Obj. $1$. **A è il distrattore più comune** (timing wrong — Methods scritto *dopo*); **D è il più sottile** (timing right, struttura right, *target rigged* — l'if-then ha solo un ramo reale). Lascio $1$–$2$ minuti.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution {.smaller}

**Correct: C.** Only C carries **all three** components of *earn complexity*, each correctly placed in time: **(i) timing — *ex ante*** (the rule is written *before* the run, so it can *constrain* the run); **(ii) baseline — simplest model on smallest sensible feature set** (logistic regression on $6$ clinically-motivated features); **(iii) target — realistic given the prevalence** (AUPRC $\ge 0.30$ at $p = 5\%$ is reachable by a $6$-feature logistic, so the *not-escalate* branch has a real chance of firing).

- **A** — wrong on **timing**. *Methods* is written *after* both runs; the rule did not govern the work, it described it. The most common failure mode in published clinical-ML papers.
- **B** — wrong on **the baseline**. Gradient boosting on $30$ features as *primary* model — no simpler baseline, no *documented failure of the simpler model* to *earn* the complexity. The committee's *"why **this** model?"* cannot be answered with population-level priors.
- **D** — wrong on **the target**. AUPRC $\ge 0.80$ on $p = 5\%$ is roughly **twice the realistic ceiling** for $30$-day ICU readmission (historical range $0.20$–$0.45$) — the if-then has *only one real branch* (escalate). A stop-criterion with only one real branch is a *plan disguised as a rule*.

*Discriminator: a binding stop-criterion is **temporally ex ante** $\wedge$ **starts simple** $\wedge$ **has a real not-escalate branch**.*

::: {.notes}
**Take-home**: la disciplina di *earn complexity* è *temporale* (prima del training) + *strutturale* (baseline semplice) + *realistica* (target raggiungibile). D è il caso che separa lo studente che ha colto la *forma sintattica* della regola da quello che ha colto la sua *forza vincolante*: in D la sintassi è perfetta (baseline + target + if-then) ma il *not-escalate* non può mai firing — escalation è già decisa.
:::

<!-- Item 02 — MCQ — Accuracy trap on p=5% -->

## Item 02 — Question {.smaller}

At Tuesday's lab meeting Sara presents a $30$-day ICU readmission classifier on the hospital extract ($5\,000$ patients · $p \approx 5\%$ · logistic on $8$ features). Closing slide: *"Excellent classification performance — logistic regression achieves $\boldsymbol{94.8\%}$ accuracy on the held-out test set."* The PI nods. You are asked to comment. **Which critique applies *accuracy trap* (R$1$) correctly?**

- **A)** *"$94.8\%$ is roughly always-predict-NO — but around one-in-five ICU patients gets readmitted, so always-predict-NO is near $\boldsymbol{80\%}$, not $95\%$. Your model is meaningfully above baseline, but I'd still like to see recall."*
- **B)** *"$94.8\%$ is essentially **always-predict-NO** on this prevalence ($1 - p = 95\%$), which has recall $0$. Accuracy alone cannot distinguish your model from always-predict-NO. Can you show **recall** (or AUPRC) on the positive class — at the threshold you would actually use in practice?"*
- **C)** *"$94.8\%$ is well above the $\boldsymbol{50\%}$ baseline a random classifier would achieve on a binary problem, so the model is clearly above chance. Next step: confirm this generalises beyond the test set."*
- **D)** *"$94.8\%$ means the model is right $94.8\%$ of the time across the patient population — that's the overall hit rate, and it's what matters for clinical deployment."*

::: {.notes}
Item $02$ — Comprehension/Application / MCQ / medium. Obj. $2$.R$1$. **A** = prevalenza letta male ($20\%$ invece di $5\%$); **C** = baseline-random ($50\%$) invece di baseline-majority; **D** = misreading clinico ("hit rate is what matters" — *plain English over formal reading*). Lascio $2$ minuti.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution {.smaller}

**Correct: B.** Only B names the **right baseline** (always-predict-NO, accuracy $1 - p = 95\%$), the **right discriminator** (recall on the positive class / AUPRC — *both immune to majority-prediction inflation*), and the **right operational anchor** (recall *at the threshold the clinician would use*).

- **A** — concept right, **prevalence wrong**. Reads $p \approx 20\%$ instead of the stated $5\%$, so always-predict-NO is mis-computed as $80\%$; Sara's $94.8\%$ is then judged *above baseline*, when in fact she is $0.2$pp *below* the always-predict-NO ceiling on this dataset.
- **C** — **wrong baseline class**. Compares to a coin-flip ($50\%$). On imbalanced data the relevant baseline is *always-predict-majority* ($1 - p = 95\%$), not the random baseline — the floor *moves with the prevalence*.
- **D** — misreads *accuracy on imbalanced data* clinically. $94.8\%$ accuracy is compatible with **recall $= 0$** on the positive class — *zero readmissions correctly identified*, all the score coming from negatives. *"Overall hit rate"* dilutes precisely the signal the clinician needs.

*Discriminator: compute the **right baseline on the right prevalence** before reading any model score.*

::: {.notes}
**Take-home**: la disciplina di *accuracy trap* su sbilanciati è *non-leggere-accuracy-da-sola*. La trappola operativa: studenti che sanno il concetto ma sbagliano il numero (A) o usano la baseline del balanced-data world (C, $50\%$) o leggono accuracy *in plain English* (D, "right is right"). Voce docente: *"$95\%$ accuracy non significa il modello è quasi perfetto — significa che la classe maggioritaria è il $95\%$, e qualunque modello che non distingua le due classi vince a quel gioco. La domanda da fare per prima, su qualunque tabella di metriche di un classificatore, è: qual è la prevalenza?"*
:::

<!-- Item 03 — MCQ — Leakage rule (Davide's sequence) -->

## Item 03 — Question {.smaller}

Davide built a $30$-day ICU readmission classifier on the same extract ($70/15/15$ train/val/test). He narrates his procedure at lab meeting and plans to report the final test number in the *Methods*.

> **Step $1$.** Logistic on *train*. Val AUPRC $= 0.25$.
> **Step $2$.** Gradient boosting on *train*. Val AUPRC $= 0.31$.
> **Step $3$.** Pick GB. CV-tune hyperparameters on *train*. Val AUPRC $= 0.34$.
> **Step $4$.** Open *test* for the first time. **Test AUPRC $= 0.29$**.
> **Step $5$.** Decide *"L$2$ looks a bit weak — nudge it up"*. Retrain. Re-open *test*. **Test AUPRC $= 0.31$**, planned as the headline.

Under R$2$, is **$0.31$** a faithful test number?

- **A) Yes.** The model was never *fit on* the test rows; reading the test twice does not change the train/test separation.
- **B) No.** *Any decision after a test-set observation converts that dataset into a training set* — the L$2$ bump in Step $5$ contaminates the test retrospectively. Neither $0.29$ nor $0.31$ is the faithful number; the fix is a **new** held-out split drawn fresh from training data.
- **C) Yes** — provided Davide reports **both** $0.29$ and $0.31$ and explains the L$2$ change. Full disclosure preserves the test's epistemic status.
- **D) Yes** — provided Davide splits a *fresh validation* set from the training pool, re-tunes L$2$ on it, then reads the **same** test split he originally used. With tuning moved off the test, $0.31$ is the legitimate result.

::: {.notes}
Item $03$ — Application / MCQ / medium-high. Obj. $2$.R$2$. **A** = legge R$2$ come "non training-on", non come "no-decision-after-observation"; **C** = trasparenza $\ne$ correttezza; **D** è il più sottile — *operationally right direction* (fresh validation è la fix per il futuro), ma il test originale è *già contaminato* — serve un *new test*, non solo una *fresh validation*. Lascio $2$–$3$ minuti.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution {.smaller}

**Correct: B.** Three components of R$2$ carry the answer:

- **The rule triggers on the *decision*, not on the *observation*.** Step $4$ alone (a single read with *no decision*) leaves the test faithful. Step $5$ is the trigger — *because* of $0.29$, Davide changes the model; that decision *uses* test information to *shape* the model.
- **Contamination is retrospective, not prospective.** Once R$2$ is violated, the original test is *no longer a test split* — no procedure applied *afterwards* restores it. The number $0.31$ is read off an already-contaminated split.
- **The fix is a *new* held-out split.** A fresh *validation* split fixes *future* tuning; it does **not** repair the already-contaminated test. The chapter's exact wording: *the test is "looked at exactly once, at the end, and never again"* — *a split looked at twice can never be that split again*.

- **A** — textbook-mechanical reading of *"test set" = "data not fit on"*. R$2$ is *operational*: test information leaks *via decisions taken on test numbers*, not only via gradient updates.
- **C** — *transparency ≠ correctness.* A disclosed biased number is still a biased number.
- **D** — **operational direction right** (praise this at the reveal), **rule wrong**. The contaminated test cannot be *legitimised* by a procedure applied later; only *replaced*. Fresh validation fixes tomorrow; a new test is what answers *today*.

*Discriminator: read R$2$ as a rule about **decisions on a dataset**, applied **retrospectively to the moment of the decision**.*

::: {.notes}
**Take-home**: la regola R$2$ non è "non fit on test" — è "*nessuna decisione presa dopo un'osservazione sul test*". Voce docente sulla D (la risposta più matura): *"hai capito la direzione operativa giusta — una fresh validation è esattamente quello che si fa per evitare leakage di tuning. Ma la regola sotto è più dura: il test che hai guardato due volte è già un training set, e non c'è una procedura applicata dopo che lo ripara. Devi sacrificare un secondo split dal training pool — non puoi recuperare il primo."*
:::

<!-- Item 04 — Applicativa — Interpretability defence -->

## Item 04 — Question {.smaller}

The audit is over. Final model: **random forest** on $\sim 12$ clinically-chosen features (validation AUPRC $= 0.32$, escalated from logistic on $6$ features at AUPRC $= 0.27$, *via the pre-registered stop-criterion*). Clinical lead has signed off on the FP/FN cost ratio; threshold set on *fresh validation* for recall $\approx 0.55$ at precision $\approx 0.40$. Defence in $5$ days.

Write the **Interpretability** section of the defence document. The section must contain:

- **(a)** which **interpretability technique** you will use, with $1$–$2$ sentences on **why this technique matches this model family** — and why *coefficients* are not available for a random forest;
- **(b)** **one sentence** stating why the choice in (a) — rather than reverting to logistic on the $6$ features and reading off coefficients — is **clinically defensible** before the ethics committee.

*Plain prose. No code, no diagrams. Write text the clinical lead could read aloud back to the committee without rephrasing.*

::: {.notes}
Item $04$ — Application / applicativa / medium-high. Obj. $3$. **C$1$** technique matching, **C$2$** technical justification, **C$3$** clinical defensibility framing — rubrica $3$ criteri $\times$ $3$ livelli. **Accetto la scelta invertita** (revert to logistic + coefficients) a Excellent se il framing clinico è ben posto. **SHAP** è bonus a Excellent se ancorata operativamente (cosa SHAP *aggiunge* a variable importance: per-patient attribution). Lascio $5$–$7$ minuti.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution (Excellent-level response) {.smaller}

> **(a)** *We will use **variable importance** computed across the random forest ensemble — a ranking of features by their average contribution to separating readmitted from non-readmitted patients. Variable importance matches the random forest family because the model's prediction is the **average across many independent trees**: no single tree's coefficient or rule is the model, so there is no per-feature weight with sign and magnitude to read off — the **built-in** route is unavailable, and a **post-hoc** ranking stands in for it. For the committee's "what does the model rely on?" we report the global ranking; for the clinical lead's "why **this** patient?" we additionally show the top-ranked features against that patient's chart, so the explanation lands on the record the clinician is already reading.*
>
> **(b)** *The random forest catches meaningfully more readmissions than the logistic baseline ($0.32$ vs $0.27$ AUPRC, an extra recall margin clinically material on this service) — and the clinical cost of a missed $30$-day readmission (re-admission, possible adverse event, longer LOS) substantially exceeds the cost of explaining each prediction with a feature-importance ranking rather than a logistic coefficient, so on this audit the patient is better served by the more accurate model with a variable-importance defence than by the simpler logistic that misses more events.*

::: {.notes}
La risposta Excellent. **C$1$** technique matching: *variable importance* per RF; rules out *coefficients*; distingue *global* (committee) da *per-patient* (clinical lead). **C$2$** technical justification: built-in/post-hoc come *regola* non come *menu*. **C$3$** clinical framing: il soggetto della frase è il *paziente*; il cost-of-failure è *clinicamente nominato* (re-admission, adverse event, LOS); il tradeoff è *posto* e *risolto dal clinical lead*. Vedi `rubrica_04_interpretability-defence.md`.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution: what the rubric rewards {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Three rubric criteria** ($3$ levels each: Base / Good / Excellent).

- **C$1$ — Technique matching.** *Variable importance* for RF; rules out *coefficients*. Excellent: distinguishes **global** (committee) from **per-patient** (clinical lead) and names a concrete per-patient route (top-ranked features against the chart, or *SHAP* as bonus if anchored).
- **C$2$ — Technical justification.** Built-in (linear → coefficients, single tree → decision path) vs post-hoc (RF/GB → variable importance, NN → SHAP/surrogate) as a $1{:}1$ **rule**, not a menu.
- **C$3$ — Clinical defensibility.** The subject is the **patient**, the cost-of-failure is *clinically named*, the tradeoff is *posed* and resolved by the clinical lead's cost ratio.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**The inverted answer — revert to logistic + coefficients — is accepted at Excellent** if matching is correct AND the clinical argument is well-posed (*"on this audit the extra recall does not justify the loss of built-in interpretability, given our cost ratio"*).

The rubric measures *applying the tradeoff as a clinical decision*, **not** picking random forest.

*Bias to avoid: penalising a logistic-baseline answer as a retreat — it is the **winning case** of the discipline when the baseline reaches the target.*

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Voce docente sull'*answer invertita*: *"se mi scrivi 'torno alla logistic perché su questo audit il guadagno di recall del random forest è sotto la soglia di accettabilità di opacità del nostro clinical lead', e poi mi nomini la soglia con il cost ratio — è una risposta Excellent. La rubrica misura se hai applicato il tradeoff come scelta clinica, non se hai scelto random forest. La logistic + coefficients è il **caso vincente** della disciplina, non un ripiego."* Bonus a Excellent per *SHAP* solo se ancorata operativamente (cosa aggiunge a variable importance: per-patient attribution che il global ranking non dà).
:::

<!-- Item 05 — Argomentativa — Critique Anna's plan -->

## Item 05 — Question {.smaller}

Anna circulates the following **project plan** by email on Friday morning for the $30$-day ICU readmission audit.

> *"Friday morning — sending the project plan.*
>
> *(1) **Model**: random forest on **all $50$ features**, since random forest is the best class for tabular clinical data.*
> *(2) **Metric**: **accuracy** on test. If $\ge \boldsymbol{90\%}$, ready for defence.*
> *(3) **Tuning**: **$5$-fold CV on combined train$+$test** — to maximise statistical power.*
> *(4) **Interpretability**: if the committee asks, I'll **read off the coefficients of each feature in the random forest**.*
>
> *Plan to defend in three weeks."*

Anna's plan contains **four** distinct violations of the chapter's three disciplines — one per numbered point. Write a critique that:

- **(a)** **names each violation** by the chapter's vocabulary (*earn complexity*, *accuracy trap*, *leakage rule*, *match interpretability $+$ clinical defensibility*), anchored to the specific point;
- **(b)** **for each violation, explains in $1$–$2$ sentences** why the clinical lead / ethics committee will reject it;
- **(c)** **proposes a corrected plan** as **one coherent revision** — written as the *order of operations* the three disciplines compose, not as four patches on Anna's original.

::: {.notes}
Item $05$ — Argumentation / argomentativa / high. **Synthesis** di Obj. $1$ + Obj. $2$ (R$1$+R$2$) + Obj. $3$. **Cascade lethal**: $90\% < 1 - p = 95\%$ — la soglia di successo di Anna è **sotto** la baseline always-predict-NO. **Bias critico della rubrica**: non penalizzare uno studente che propone *logistic + coefficients* nella revisione — è il *winning case* della disciplina. Lascio $7$–$8$ minuti.
:::

## Item 05 — Solution (a) $+$ (b) {.smaller}

**(a) Four violations, one per point.**

- **Point $(1)$ violates *earn complexity* (Obj. $1$).** RF on all $50$ features as **primary** model; no logistic baseline; no pre-registered target; no stop-criterion *ex ante*. The justification *"RF is the best class"* is a **population-level prior**, not a project-level argument.
- **Point $(2)$ violates *accuracy trap* (Obj. $2$, R$1$).** Accuracy on $p = 5\%$, with success threshold $\ge 90\%$ — Anna has not compared $90\%$ to the always-predict-NO baseline of $\boldsymbol{1 - p = 95\%}$. **Her success criterion sits *below* the baseline that does nothing.**
- **Point $(3)$ violates *leakage rule* (Obj. $2$, R$2$).** $5$-fold CV on combined train$+$test uses the test to choose hyperparameters; *any decision after a test-set observation converts the test into a training set*. **There is no test left to read at the end.**
- **Point $(4)$ violates *match interpretability $+$ clinical defensibility* (Obj. $3$).** RFs have no coefficients (the prediction is averaged across trees); the chapter's mapping for ensembles is **variable importance**. *"If the committee asks"* is an **afterthought** — the defence is owed to the patient *before* the committee asks.

**(b) Why each breaks the defence.**

The earn-complexity violation gives the committee no answer to *"why this model?"* — only a general-superiority claim. The accuracy-trap violation collapses Anna's *"ready"* threshold to **below** what doing nothing scores. The leakage violation removes the held-out evidence that answers *"why should I trust it on my next patient?"*. The interpretability violation breaks the defence **twice** — the matching error (no coefficients on RF) **and** the framing error (interpretability as afterthought, not as patient-owed argument).

::: {.notes}
Slide $1$/$2$ della soluzione di item $05$. La *cascade lethal* — $90\% < 95\%$ — è il segnale di Excellent sul C$2$ della rubrica (operational diagnosis). Lo studente che la nomina ha letto i due punti $(1)$ e $(2)$ *insieme*, non come violazioni isolate.
:::

## Item 05 — Solution (c): the corrected plan {.smaller}

> *Before any training, write the stop-criterion: **baseline $=$ logistic regression on $5$–$10$ clinically-chosen features** (e.g. age, ICU LOS, Charlson, prior $90$-day admissions, eGFR, $\#$ medications); **target $=$ AUPRC $\ge 0.30$** (or recall $\ge 0.55$ at precision $\ge 0.40$) on a held-out **validation** split; **escalation $=$ if the baseline misses the target, escalate to random forest on a wider clinical feature set; otherwise ship the baseline**.*
>
> *The metric is **not accuracy** — AUPRC or recall-at-precision, because $5\%$ prevalence makes accuracy uninterpretable; the threshold is set by the **cost ratio the clinical lead signs off on**, not by an arbitrary $90\%$.*
>
> *Hyperparameter tuning runs on a **fresh validation split** drawn from the training pool; the test set is **sealed in a separate folder until the day of the defence** and opened **exactly once**, on that day.*
>
> *Interpretability matches whatever model finally ships: **coefficients** if the logistic baseline reaches the target (which on this audit is the **most defensible** outcome — built-in interpretability, simpler model, smaller per-patient risk per unit error); **variable importance $+$ top-ranked features against this patient's chart** if escalation is required, with the tradeoff posed explicitly to the clinical lead.*
>
> *The plan does not predetermine the model; it predetermines the **discipline** that decides between models. The three disciplines compose — **start simple, measure honestly, defend clinically** — as an **order of operations**, not as four independent patches.*

::: {.notes}
Slide $2$/$2$ — la revisione corretta. **Excellent-level marker**: il piano non predetermina il modello ma la *disciplina*. La frase di chiusura — *"three disciplines compose; not four patches"* — è il take-home del capitolo intero. **Bias da non commettere**: se uno studente propone *logistic + coefficients* come outcome finale, è il **winning case** della disciplina (built-in, simpler, smaller risk per unit error), non un ripiego — vedi `rubrica_05_critique-the-plan.md`. Voce docente di chiusura del corso, dopo l'item: *"queste tre discipline non sono regole d'arte separate. Sono un ordine di operazioni. Senza la prima, il modello complicato è una scommessa non motivata. Senza la seconda, qualunque numero è dubbio. Senza la terza, qualunque sistema è indifendibile al primo paziente che chiede 'perché mi ha dimesso?'."*
:::
